body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The information technology industry is driving massive growth in global electricity demand, which is set to rise by more than 10,000 TWh over the next ten years. For this electricity to reach demand hubs, grids around the world will need urgent upgrades. In its World Energy Outlook released this week, the International Energy Agency once again joined the growing chorus of forecasters warning that data centers are becoming a major drain on electricity supply. Some of these warnings and community opposition to new facilities that may bring their electricity bills higher helped tip the midterm scales in Democrats’ favor. Others are casting doubts about the AI revolution's potential for success if data center operators cannot secure enough electricity for all their planned facilities. The IEA noted the importance of keeping electricity affordable as pro-transition governments try to boost the share of electricity in final energy consumption. “Successful electrification means keeping electricity available and affordable, putting the emphasis on effective use and expansion of grids, and greater operational flexibility in power systems,” the International Energy Agency wrote in the executive summary of its report. It then went on to add that while AI is widely expected to help with things like energy efficiency and grid optimization, “for the moment, surging demand from data centres is amplifying strains in some markets and supply chains.” The financial side of the energy problem with data centers is the most serious one. Net-zero ambitions already required massive spend on new transmission lines before the AI craze began. Now, the tab is just going to go higher as data centers join other demand centers that need to be supplied with reliable, hopefully low-carbon electricity, per the IEA’s and net-zero governments’ agenda. Meanwhile, as it emerges that data center operators tend to split the grid connection bill generously with nearby residents, opposition is likely to grow as well. Related: China’s Oil Imports from Persian Gulf Jump to Wartime High A study from Cornell University this month revealed that wholesale prices for electricity across four regions in the U.S. rose because of demand from data centers. However, the study also found that these data centers’ operators only paid for 38% of the infrastructure costs related to their facilities’ connection to and use of the grid. The remainder fell on local communities. In money terms, data center operators paid $3.12 billion, and households paid $5.13 billion. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that there were some 58 GW in new data centers under construction across the United States, citing data from Cleanview. That total represented 577 locations, whose demand for electricity the WSJ compared to six times the electricity demand of New York City at its peak. A fifth of that total is being built in Texas--but Texas just got a change of the guard, and the newcomers are not big fans of data centers. “We need an immediate moratorium on data centers to last until the legislature can meet to put in place real protections so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities,” Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s campaign website said before the election. On that, she was in agreement with predecessor Greg Abbott, who earlier this year banned new data center approvals to investigate whether they were having a negative impact on energy prices and other issues. Whether the data center building boom slows or not, there is already plenty of new demand for electricity coming from these facilities and, in countries run by strong pro-transition politicians, the drive to replace baseload electricity with wind and solar continues

title: India's GDP Growth Draws Global Attention as Trump Cites Economic Success to Criticise US Fed - Khalsa Vox
body: India's strong economic growth has found a prominent mention in American political discourse, with US President Donald Trump highlighting the country's 7 per cent GDP expansion while criticising the Federal Reserve's interest rate policies. Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, November 20, Trump pointed to India's economic performance as an example of how favourable borrowing conditions could support growth. His remarks placed India's economic momentum at the centre of a debate over US monetary policy. "If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP," Trump said, contrasting the Indian economy with the United States. The American President argued that the US could achieve significantly higher growth if its central bank reduced borrowing costs. He suggested that American GDP growth could potentially reach 15 to 20 per cent, although such figures represented his own projections rather than established economic forecasts. Trump also accused the Federal Reserve of being politically influenced, claiming that interest rates remained unnecessarily high despite positive economic indicators. For India, the comparison marks a notable moment of international recognition, with the world's largest economy looking towards India's growth performance during a discussion about its own economic prospects. India has remained among the fastest-growing major economies, supported by domestic economic activity and its expanding presence in global markets. Its growth trajectory has attracted international attention as major economies navigate inflationary pressures, uncertain trade conditions and changing monetary policies. Trump's reference is particularly significant because India was presented as a positive economic comparison rather than merely as an emerging market. The remarks underscore the growing visibility of Indian economic performance in global policy discussions. However, differences between the two economies remain substantial. Interest rate decisions depend on inflation, employment conditions, financial stability and other domestic factors. Lower borrowing costs alone do not guarantee faster economic growth. The Federal Reserve continues to face inflationary pressures, with US annual personal consumption expenditures inflation reportedly reaching 3.6 per cent in September, above its 2 per cent target. Nevertheless, the White House remarks have brought renewed attention to India's economic trajectory. As India strengthens its position in the international economic landscape, Trump's invocation of its growth rate reflects how the country's performance is increasingly becoming part of conversations about global competitiveness and economic policymaking. The comparison also reinforces India's rising profile as a major economy whose growth figures command attention beyond its borders.

title: US President Trump lauds India’s economic growth & low interest rates - The Indian Awaaz
body: US President Donald Trump has praised India’s low interest rates and strong economic growth. He cited India as an example while criticising the US Federal Reserve for damaging the American economy by keeping interest rates high despite strong economic performance. Mr Trump made the comparison at a news conference in Washington last night after returning from a four-day visit to Asia. Referring to India’s economic growth of around seven per cent, President Trump argued that the US economy, currently growing at around four per cent, could expand by 14 to 20 per cent if the Federal Reserve lowered borrowing costs instead of keeping interest rates high. He also said that the United States should be able to borrow money at lower interest rates than any other country. Mr Trump accused the Federal Reserve of taking a political approach to monetary policy and keeping borrowing costs high despite strong economic indicators. The US President further claimed that a 1 percentage point cut in interest rates could save the country 650 billion dollars in debt payments. He also highlighted rising investments in manufacturing, saying factory activity had expanded for ten consecutive months and investment in new equipment had increased by 21 per cent this year. Mr Trump credited his tariff policies with encouraging companies such as Audi and Toyota to invest in manufacturing in the United States. He also pointed to falling oil and petrol prices as signs of economic improvement. He said future petrol prices could depend, in part, on a possible agreement between the United States and Iran. The US Federal Reserve determines interest rates based on economic conditions, particularly inflation and employment, with the twin objectives of maintaining price stability and supporting maximum employment.

title: Peterson: Nvidia’s leadership crisis tests the chipmaker’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
summary: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector. A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion. But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said. "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said. Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against. And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts. In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy. "I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit. Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years. The market is still forecast to record a sixth straight annual deficit, but a smaller one, of 35 million ounces, against 54 million ounces in 2025. Industry is the biggest source of silver demand, and it is shrinking this year. Industrial use is expected to drop 3% to 640 million ounces, though that is still about 22% above 2019. Against this backdrop, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is little changed near $83.00 per barrel in Friday's Asian trading, following modest gains in the previous session. Missile attacks on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, were launched on Thursday by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement. At the same time, Iran's navy said two oil tankers had struck naval mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz. The incidents intensified concerns about interruptions to transit through the critical shipping route. Signs of substantial production growth and possible market surpluses nevertheless persist despite the regional incidents. According to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, flows through the Strait of Hormuz have in fact climbed to record levels as Middle Eastern output recovers. Separately, a trilateral agreement to expand the production and supply of refined petroleum products was reached on Thursday by the United States, China, and Russia. For the current quarter, the International Energy Agency forecasts a global supply surplus of roughly 2 million barrels per day. Goldman Sachs has similarly warned of a possible oversupply next year. On Iran, President Donald Trump said he was in no hurry to make a decision, although recent reports indicate an increasing likelihood of further US strikes. Among the crude oil varieties traded internationally, WTI, short for West Texas Intermediate, is one of three major types alongside Brent and Dubai Crude. Its relatively low gravity and sulphur content earn it the descriptions “light” and “sweet”, respectively. These characteristics make it a high-quality oil that is easy to refine. Produced in the United States, WTI is distributed through the Cushing hub, known as “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. The oil market uses WTI as a benchmark, and its price is regularly cited in the media. Supply and demand primarily determine WTI oil prices, as they do for other assets. Stronger global growth can lift demand, while weaker growth can have the reverse effect. On the supply side, political instability, wars and sanctions can cause disruptions that affect prices. Decisions by OPEC, the group of major oil-producing countries, are another important influence. WTI crude is also sensitive to the US Dollar's value because oil is traded predominantly in US Dollars. A weaker US Dollar can therefore make oil more affordable, while a stronger currency can have the opposite effect. WTI oil prices respond to the weekly oil inventory reports from the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA), as stock movements reflect shifts in supply and demand. Falling inventories may signal stronger demand and push oil prices higher; rising stocks may point to increased supply and weigh on prices. The API releases its report each Tuesday, followed by the EIA the next day. The two sets of findings are generally similar, coming within 1% of one another 75% of the time. As the EIA is a government agency, its figures are regarded as more reliable. At meetings held twice a year, the 12 oil-producing nations belonging to OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) jointly set production quotas for member countries. WTI oil prices frequently react to these decisions: lower quotas can constrain supply and lift prices, whereas increased production has the reverse effect. title: Goldman Sachs sees crude easing to $78 by late 2027 despite ongoing West Asia tensions. Here's why - Business Today
body: Benchmark Brent crude is projected to fall from $93 per barrel to $78 by early December 2027 — and average $88 across the year — as West Asia producers bypass Strait of Hormuz disruptions and push the global oil market into a 2 million barrel-per-day surplus, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The forecast assumes no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in the war in Iran and no re-escalation causing major long-term damage to oil infrastructure. Analysts estimate the market already tipped into surplus in October 2026 after Persian Gulf crude exports climbed 2 million barrels per day from the prior month to recover to their 2025 average. Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research at Goldman Sachs, notes that oil prices have risen less sharply than expected given the duration of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz due to rapid adjustments across supply chains and consumption. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and continued market adaptation,” Struyven wrote in the report released recently. Even as Goldman Sachs projects easing prices later in 2027, analysts caution that volatility remains active. Near-term upside risks include intensified shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a rebuilt geopolitical risk premium — alongside potential refinery strikes, heavy planned maintenance, and refiners shifting output from gasoline to diesel, which led Goldman to recommend long positions in European gasoline for summer 2027 as a hedge. Conversely, stronger supply, weaker demand, or a smaller risk premium than assumed could weigh further on prices. International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol cautioned that the crisis — which the IEA's World Energy Outlook estimates has caused cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas — would leave deeper scars the longer it persists, despite producer and consumer resilience. Markets will next watch OPEC+ ministers when they meet on November 29 to weigh 2027 production policy. The International Energy Agency (IEA), in its World Energy Outlook 2026 report published the same day, said disruptions at Hormuz had removed 2.8 billion barrels of Middle East oil as of the end of October. Those products hold major implications for the prices of gasoline, plastics and European electricity, among a host of other goods. A commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said late Monday that the Strait of Hormuz had been closed, according to remarks made on Iranian State TV. Here’s what to know about the Strait of Hormuz and why it matters for oil and gas prices: The Strait of Hormuz is a waterway that runs along the southern coast of Iran and the northern coast of Oman. The passage marks the only shipping route that stretches from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, making it a key travel hub for goods originating in oil-rich Gulf countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Iran. At its narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz is just 21 miles wide. In 2024, an average of about 20 million barrels of oil per day passed through the Strait of Hormuz, which amounts to roughly 20% of liquid petroleum consumed worldwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration , or EIA, a government agency. title: Gold slides to lowest level since September 2025, silver crashes nearly 4%: What's driving the selloff? - Livemint
body: Gold and silver prices plunged in US trade on Friday, dragged down by a technology-driven stock market selloff , mounting concerns over global growth and expectations of further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Gold fell towards $3,500 an ounce , hitting its lowest level since September 2025, while silver plunged nearly 4% as investors pulled back from commodities amid deteriorating risk sentiment. According to Kitco, spot gold was trading at $3,537.90 an ounce at 5 p.m. ET on Friday, down $86.30, or 2.38%, while spot silver stood at $41.120, falling $1.637, or 3.83%. Gold touched an intraday low of $3,502.93, while silver slipped to $40.660. The selloff came despite a weaker US dollar and declining Treasury yields, which would typically support precious metals, suggesting that broader portfolio liquidation and concerns about the economic outlook were overriding traditional market drivers. The sharp decline in US equities triggered selling across asset classes as investors reassessed valuations of artificial intelligence companies, heavy technology spending and the sustainability of returns from AI investments. The S&P 500 plunged 3.70% on Friday to close at 6,910.39, falling more than 10% from its October 6 record high and entering correction territory. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.28% to 22,617.73, turning negative for the year, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. The selloff extended losses for the week, with the Nasdaq declining approximately 10%, the S&P 500 losing 8.6% and the Dow falling around 8%. The broader market weakness encouraged investors to reduce exposure to risk assets, with gold and silver also facing liquidation rather than benefiting from increased demand for safe havens. Expectations surrounding the Federal Reserve 's December 8-9 policy meeting remain a key factor influencing precious metals. Minutes from the Fed's October meeting indicated that nearly all policymakers anticipated further interest rate increases, with persistent inflation remaining a major concern. Markets continued to favour a 25-basis-point increase in December, although expectations for a larger 50-basis-point move diminished. Higher interest rates generally weigh on gold because bullion does not offer interest income, making it less attractive relative to yield-bearing assets. However, Treasury yields declined on Friday, with the 10-year yield easing towards 4.94% and the two-year yield falling near 4.65%. The dollar also softened, but neither development provided meaningful support to precious metals as investors continued unwinding positions. Silver's sharper decline reflects its dual role as an investment asset and an industrial metal. Concerns about slowing global economic growth, weaker manufacturing activity and reduced industrial demand have increased pressure on silver. The metal's exposure to sectors such as electronics, solar energy and manufacturing makes it more vulnerable to deteriorating economic expectations than gold. The technology-led market selloff and weakening industrial commodities further amplified silver's losses. Ongoing US-Iran tensions, risks surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial shipping continue to underpin geopolitical uncertainty. However, these risks have failed to offset concerns about interest rates, economic growth and financial-market liquidation. Investors will watch upcoming US economic data and Federal Reserve commentary for fresh clues on interest rates and growth. The outlook for precious metals will depend on whether the current selloff eases or deepens amid continued uncertainty over monetary policy and global markets. title: Fed Likely to Keep Raising Rates Despite Stock Selloff - JournalArta
body: Economists expect the Federal Reserve to continue raising interest rates even after US stocks entered correction territory. They say policymakers are focused on inflation, though a deeper selloff or financial-market distress could change their assessment. Federal Reserve officials are likely to keep raising interest rates despite a US stock-market correction, economists said. Major indexes have fallen more than 10% from recent highs, but the central bank remains focused on inflation. Economists said years of stock gains have left room for a decline without necessarily disrupting consumer spending. A deeper selloff or signs of financial distress could change that calculation. “At this point, I don’t think it is material for them. It can become material, but we’re not there yet,” said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC Capital Markets. The S&P 500 remains positive for 2026 and has returned 100% over the past four years. The Fed raised rates by a quarter-point in September, its first increase in three years, to fight rising consumer prices. It held rates steady in October, partly because of stock-market weakness, according to minutes of the meeting. Almost all officials nevertheless anticipated further increases, the minutes showed. Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said most officials were looking past market volatility. Shenfeld said stocks could matter to the Fed if losses substantially reduced household wealth or signaled trouble ahead for the economy. He said both were less likely after the market’s gains over the past few years. Nancy Van Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said a deep selloff could prompt high-income consumers to cut spending. Spending by wealthy Americans has been a key driver of consumer spending this year. Economists broadly expect a December rate increase after hot October inflation readings, but their forecasts diverge after that. They also differ over how much financial-market weakness could alter the Fed’s plans. Michael Gapen, chief US economist at Morgan Stanley, expects a gradual approach: a pause in January followed by another increase in March. Other economists expect increases in December, January and March before a pause. Shenfeld expects two increases, in December and January. Andrew Hollenhorst, US chief economist at Citi, expects an early December increase, followed by a hold and eventual cuts later next year. Some economists worry the Fed could raise rates too far as it seeks to reach its 2% inflation target. Shenfeld said officials were concerned inflation could become entrenched at 3% rather than 2%. Fed officials discussed scenarios involving a possible selloff linked to a reversal of optimism about artificial intelligence, the October meeting minutes showed. Scott Anderson, chief US economist at BMO Capital Markets, said officials would watch for bank distress and problems in financial markets. He said the biggest concern would be “systemic dislocation” in those markets. Such disruption might require special credit lines to inject money into markets, Anderson said. He compared that possibility with measures taken during the 2008 financial crisis and at the start of the COVID pandemic in 2020.

title: [COVER STORY] 'AI spending binge puts Samsung, SK at risk of memory price collapse' - The Korea Times
body: Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could face a sharp memory price decline if hyperscalers scale back the artificial intelligence (AI) spending that has driven the current chip boom, according to a renowned U.S. semiconductor analyst. Jim Handy, founder and general director at Objective Analysis, said in an interview with The Korea Times that the surge in memory prices — caused by a sharp increase in demand — is “temporary,” echoing concerns among some Korean analysts that the current memory cycle may be nearing its peak. “I do not think that AI demand is growing that quickly, so they are likely to slow their spending at some point, and that will cause memory prices to collapse,” Handy said. Although the timing of a downturn is difficult to predict, memory prices could eventually fall back to 2024 levels once demand weakens, he said. Handy has raised particular concerns over the scale of spending by hyperscalers such as Google, Meta, Amazon and OpenAI. These companies are spending roughly 40 percent of their revenue on capital expenditures, including massive investments in AI computing infrastructure, he said. "Such spending is sustainable only if AI demand continues to grow rapidly enough to justify the investment. If that growth slows, the big tech firms could sharply reduce capital spending, weakening demand for memory chips and creating an oversupply in the market," he said. Many Korean analysts have focused on rising production levels as the main threat to prices. Handy, however, argued that the more serious risk could come from the demand side if AI investment fails to maintain its current pace. The warning came amid growing investor concerns as to the steep stock fall of the two Korean chipmakers. Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix plunged about 33 percent and 34 percent, respectively, over the past three months until Friday, with the latest sell-off amplifying concerns that the memory boom may be nearing its peak. Chipmakers have benefited from a sharp recovery in chip prices, as AI server demand has lifted orders for high-bandwidth memory and other high-end chips. Their strong pricing power has driven a significant improvement in earnings, helping Samsung Electronics post the world’s highest quarterly operating profit in the third quarter. Buoyed by robust earnings and strong memory demand, their stock prices soared through June, but momentum has slowed. The latest stock fall has also triggered market fears over the sustainability of the AI investment boom. The concern is particularly significant for Samsung and SK hynix, whose recent earnings growth has been heavily supported by soaring memory prices. If hyperscalers cut spending, the resulting demand shock could reverse the pricing power that has driven their record profitability. “Production levels are limited by demand projections made two years ago,” he said. “Since demand has grown higher than these projections, we have a shortage — and that shortage has driven prices very high. That growth is temporary, and sometime in the future prices will fall back to where they were in 2024,” Handy stated. Handy also warned that the downturn could be severe. If the current cycle follows the pattern of previous memory supercycles, chipmakers’ gross margins could fall from above 80 percent to near zero within roughly two quarters. For Samsung and SK hynix, the key risk is therefore no longer simply whether they can keep up with AI-driven demand, according to Handy. It is whether that demand will remain strong enough to absorb the enormous amount of capacity and investment being built around it.

title: Dan Ives Just Delivered Great News for AI Stocks. Here’s the Part That Matters. - Yahoo Finance
body: Artificial intelligence stocks are taking an absolute beating this month. The Nasdaq-100 is down 13% since the beginning of November, and the losses seem to be accelerating. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) dropped 37%, Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is off by 33%, and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is down 20%. It hasn't been pretty. But analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, isn't abandoning his bullish outlook. In a post on X on Friday, Ives identified seven factors contributing to "a perfect storm" that's driving the sell-off. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » And here's the most important part of his message: "The $4 trillion AI build-out is still happening," he wrote, "and our tech thesis into 2027 remains." That's key -- particularly for investors who are nervous about their portfolios right now. And if Ives is right, this is also an opportunity to buy tech stocks at a discount. In his social media post, Ives said the Democrats' midterm election victory is creating uncertainty for AI stocks, as investors worry that Washington will impose tougher restrictions on AI development and data center construction. He also singled out the sudden resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang "in his black eye moment." Huang was forced out after the board began investigating his affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for Beijing. Meanwhile, regulatory concerns involving China, persistent inflation, and the prospect of additional Federal Reserve interest rate increases have weighed on technology stocks. Ives also pointed to forced selling and investment funds suffering losses that have reduced their ability to buy shares. Ives even singled out Anthropic 's (NASDAQ:ANT) successful IPO on Nov. 19, speculating that investors shifted money out of tech stocks and into the newly public AI company. A perfect storm, indeed. But here's the thing -- none of those factors mean that customers are slowing their AI spending. And the demand for computing capacity remains sky-high. That's why analysts, including Ives, have projected that capital expenditures and AI spending will reach $4 trillion. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue in its fiscal third quarter of 2027, up 103% from a year ago. And data center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110%. But perhaps the most important thing is that Nvidia increased its forecast for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. And notably, that outlook came in the first earnings report since Huang's departure. Management expects demand to accelerate even faster. Alphabet is seeing similar strength in cloud computing. Google Cloud revenue in the third quarter was $30.7 billion, up 103% from a year ago. Operating income more than tripled to $11.1 billion, and its backlog reached $561 billion. Those figures suggest businesses are still signing contracts for computing infrastructure, even as investors question whether AI spending has gone too far. And Anthropic's IPO prospectus offers another example. The Claude developer has committed to spending at least $110 billion with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and $121.3 billion with Google under long-term cloud computing arrangements. That's an enormous amount of planned infrastructure spending from just one AI company. Ives can't predict when the technology sell-off will end. But his central argument deserves attention: The market's enthusiasm for AI stocks has cooled considerably, while the companies supplying the infrastructure continue to report massive demand. For investors, that means don't panic over this month's slide in tech stocks. And if you're feeling opportunistic, this could be an ideal time to add to positions while prices remain depressed. In 2013, he wrote, the fear was that cheap Android phones would wreck Apple’s margins. title: China Switched to Making Its Own Chips “At All Costs.” That Shrinks Nvidia’s China Upside - TIKR.com
body: President Donald Trump came back from Shenzhen with what sounded like good news for Nvidia ( NVDA ) . “In two years or three years, I would, if I were here, I would say, go ahead. You can now sell Blackwells because they’ll have something else,” he told Fox News. The problem is that China has spent years making sure it will have something else too. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, said it on this week’s episode of the Odd Lots podcast : “China’s kind of like switched from, yeah, we should probably make our own chips to we must at all costs.” You can already see that at Alibaba ( BABA ) , which is building its own AI chips. It’s also why ASML ( ASML ) and Applied Materials ( AMAT ) are still selling China plenty of equipment, for now. Nvidia’s outlook with its third-quarter results this month is blunt: “We are not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook.” Analysts expect Nvidia’s revenue to keep climbing fast anyway: Customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong brought in $19.7 billion in the year ended January 2026, down from $25.0 billion the year before. Both include gaming chips. Even a full $25 billion a year from China would be under 4% of the $726 billion analysts expect for the year ending January 2028.
